Teaching reflects what society itself demands; it necessitates that disorder ─ of students and teachers alike, of mind, behavior, and environment ─ yield to its opposite.
(A) Effective teaching requires that, failing their own self-imposed order, students experience the imposition of some outer order so that inner order may develop.
(B) That is, good teaching requires that teachers and students subject themselves to external and internal control so that learning can take place.

(C) This means in practice, for instance, that the goals of classes and courses be clearly set, that they be explained and justified, that the manner of achieving them be clear, that the presentation of materials conducive to reaching them be appropriate, and that all activities be directed somehow to their attainment.
(D) Above all, it implies structured industry ─ study and activity that are oriented toward a goal and pursued with perseverance and method.

(E) It means, too, that students take up their own obligation to maintain the conditions under which learning occurs: quiet in their classrooms, respect for and courtesy toward others, civility of language and behavior, and the like.

When we lecture, scold, yell, or criticize, when we say something positive but in a sarcastic tone, or when we try to make our kids feel guilty, it activates their amygdala, triggering their stress response and putting them into a defensive, rigid, reactive state.
(A) For this reason, the researchers Suniya Luthar and John Gottman say that "bad is stronger than good" when it comes to communicating with children and teens.
(B) Even more basic, when we say no or don't, it releases stress chemicals in our kids' brains (and in ours) that are associated with fear and anger.
(C) Conversely, positive words like yes, love, and peace activate systems in the prefrontal cortex that are related to emotional regulation.
(D) The problem is that negative words like no and don't have a more powerful effect on kids than positive words.

(E) Functional brain imaging research has shown that even seeing the word no on a screen for less than a second while you're lying in an MRI scanner will cause your brain to suddenly release dozens of stress-producing hormones and neurotransmitters.
